opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic issue is that robot actions are continuous, and they're often multimodal. If you think about language, you have discrete tokens, and a softmax over a vocabulary gives you a really nice, expressive way to represent any distribution you want. But with robots, you're outputting joint angles, end-effector positions, gripper commands, and you're doing that at high frequency, maybe 50 times a second. So you need something that can represent a rich, continuous distribution over a whole chunk of future actions.

The naive thing is to regress actions with a Gaussian or mean-squared-error loss. That works okay when there's one right answer. But often there isn't. If you're going around an obstacle, you could go left or right. If you average those two, you go straight into the obstacle. So you really need a model that can capture multiple modes, and diffusion and flow matching are very good at that. They've been proven out in image generation, where you also have high-dimensional continuous outputs with very complex distributions.

Flow matching in particular is nice because it's relatively simple to train and fairly efficient at inference time, which matters a lot when you have to run a controller in real time. In our models, like pi-zero, we take a vision-language model backbone that carries all the semantic knowledge from web-scale pretraining, and attach what we call an action expert that uses flow matching to produce action chunks. So the VLM handles the "what should I do" part, and the flow matching head handles the "how exactly do I move my body" part, with the precision and smoothness that dexterous manipulation needs.

There are alternatives. We've also worked on tokenizing actions, for example with the FAST tokenizer, which compresses action sequences using a frequency-domain representation so you can train them like language tokens. That has some advantages, like faster training. But a continuous generative model is a very natural fit for the problem, especially for fine-grained, high-frequency control.

r001.rationale: The response says the flow-matching head provides the precision and smoothness needed for dexterous manipulation, identifying action precision as a reason for using it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the short answer is that actions are really hard to represent well, and the naive thing you might do, which is just regress onto the action, turns out to work surprisingly badly.

Let me unpack that a bit. When you train a robot policy from demonstration data, you're basically trying to learn a mapping from observations to actions. The obvious thing is to say, okay, I have a neural network, I'll have it output the action, and I'll train it with a mean squared error loss on the actions the human took. The problem is that human demonstrations are multimodal. If I'm reaching around an obstacle to grab a cup, sometimes I'll go left and sometimes I'll go right, and both are perfectly fine. But if you train with mean squared error, the network learns the average of those two things, and the average is going straight into the obstacle. So you get this kind of mushy, averaged-out behavior that doesn't correspond to anything that any demonstrator actually did.

And this gets worse when you think about action chunks, where you're predicting not just one action but a whole sequence of maybe fifty actions into the future. Now the space of plausible things is really diverse, and you really want something that can represent a complex distribution over that space rather than a single point estimate.

So that's where diffusion and flow matching come in. These are generative models. They're the same machinery that people use to generate images. And the thing they're really good at is representing complicated, high-dimensional, multimodal distributions. Instead of outputting the action directly, you output a vector field that tells you how to transform noise into a sample from the action distribution. At inference time you start with noise, you integrate along that field for a few steps, and you get out an action chunk that looks like something a human actually did, not an average of several things humans did.

There's also a more practical reason, which is that this plays really nicely with large pretrained vision-language models. In the pi-zero work, for example, we have a VLM backbone that handles the images and the language, and then there's a separate action expert that does the flow matching. The flow matching part is fast enough that you can run it at real-time control rates, around fifty hertz, which matters a lot for dexterous things like folding laundry. Discretizing actions into tokens, which is the other main alternative, works, and we've used it too, but it tends to be slower for high-frequency control and you lose some precision from the quantization.

I'd say flow matching specifically versus diffusion is a smaller distinction. It's a cleaner formulation, a bit simpler to implement and tune, and you can get away with fewer integration steps. But conceptually they're doing the same thing, which is giving you a way to express "here is a distribution over good things to do" rather than "here is the one thing to do."

r001.rationale: The response says tokenizing actions loses precision through quantization, while flow matching supports high-frequency control for dexterous tasks such as folding laundry.

astra-6.text:
The basic reason is that there are many different ways to do the same task, and you want your policy to be able to represent those different possibilities. Suppose a robot needs to reach around an obstacle. It could go to the left or to the right. If you train a model to predict an action with a squared-error loss, it might average those two possibilities and go straight into the obstacle. You want to pick one of those behaviors, rather than average them together.

Diffusion and flow matching give you a fairly expressive way to model that kind of distribution. You start with noise and iteratively transform it into an action, or, more commonly, a sequence of actions, conditioned on what the robot sees and what you want it to do. That lets you represent several distinct strategies while producing a coherent sequence within any particular sample.

You could also discretize actions and generate them autoregressively, much like a language model generates tokens. But robot actions are naturally continuous, and you often want to generate a whole chunk of them together. These methods are a convenient fit for that. There’s a computational tradeoff because you have to run the generation process, but the attraction is really the combination of expressiveness and being able to model continuous action sequences.

r001.rationale: The response says diffusion and flow matching suit continuous action sequences, but it does not identify the precision required for dexterous robot control as a reason.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic issue is that there can be many different good actions in the same situation. If a robot is reaching around an obstacle, it could go to the left or to the right. If you train a model to predict an action with a squared-error loss, it might average those two possibilities and go straight into the obstacle. What you want is a model that represents the distribution of possible actions, so that it can pick one coherent way of doing the task.

Diffusion and flow matching give us a very effective way to represent those distributions, particularly when the output is a whole sequence of actions. You start with noise and progressively transform it into an action sequence, conditioned on what the robot sees and what you want it to do. That lets you capture dependencies across time, as well as different possible strategies.

They’re also fairly straightforward to train. You don’t have to explicitly calculate the probability of every action sequence. You train the network to denoise, or to predict a vector field that takes noise toward the actions in your data.

There is a tradeoff at inference time, because generating an action can require multiple network evaluations, and robots have timing constraints. But these methods give you a useful combination of expressive distributions and stable training. It’s not that robot actions intrinsically have to be represented with diffusion; it’s that this turns out to be a good practical tool for learning the kinds of action distributions we need.

r001.rationale: The response explains multimodal action distributions and practical benefits, but does not identify the precision required for dexterous robot control as a reason for using these methods.
